data.title: Asteatotic eczema — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Asteatotic eczema** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. What is asteatotic eczema? Synonyms?**
- Eczema arising on very dry (xerotic) skin with fine cracks — eczema craquelé, winter itch, xerotic eczema
- Commonest in elderly on shins, also arms, trunk

**Q2. Classify eczemas (PYQ).**
- Endogenous: atopic, seborrhoeic, discoid (nummular), asteatotic, pompholyx, lichen simplex chronicus, venous (stasis), juvenile plantar dermatosis, pityriasis alba
- Exogenous: irritant contact, allergic contact, photoallergic/phototoxic, infective (infectious eczematoid), dermatophytide/id reactions
- Morphological stage: acute (vesicles, oozing), subacute (scaling, crusts), chronic (lichenification)

**Q3. Why does the skin crack?**
- Reduced stratum corneum lipids (ceramides, cholesterol, free fatty acids) and natural moisturising factor with age → loss of water, shrinkage of corneocytes → fissures in a 'crazy-paving'/dried river bed pattern; irritant inflammation follows

**Q4. Predisposing factors.**
- Ageing, low humidity (winter, air-conditioning, heating), frequent hot baths and soaps, diuretics, hypothyroidism, malnutrition (zinc, essential fatty acids), hospitalisation
- Drugs: statins, retinoids, cimetidine, EGFR inhibitors
- Widespread sudden asteatotic eczema in elderly may be paraneoplastic (lymphoma) or with hypothyroidism

**Q5. Clinical features.**
- Dry, scaly, itchy skin with superficial polygonal fissures and red edges (crazy-paving); later erythematous plaques, excoriations, secondary infection
- Worse in winter, improves in summer

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Ichthyosis vulgaris (since childhood, family history), stasis dermatitis (varicose veins, haemosiderin), nummular eczema, allergic contact dermatitis to topical medicaments, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, xerosis from renal failure, scabies in elderly

**Q7. Management.**
- Reduce bathing frequency, lukewarm water, soap substitutes, pat dry
- Liberal emollients immediately after bath (soak-and-seal); urea 5–10%, lactic acid 12% (avoid on fissured inflamed skin — sting)
- Mild–moderate potency topical steroid ointment for 1–2 weeks for inflamed areas; humidifier, cotton clothing
- Treat associated hypothyroidism, review drugs

**Q8. What is the role of essential fatty acids? (PYQ)**
- Linoleic acid is needed for ceramide synthesis and barrier function; deficiency (TPN, malabsorption) gives dry scaly eczematous skin, alopecia, poor wound healing — corrected by EFA supplementation/topical oils

**Q9. How does ageing affect the skin barrier?**
- Reduced epidermal lipid synthesis (ceramides, cholesterol), reduced filaggrin/NMF, slower barrier recovery, reduced sebum and sweat, higher pH — dry, itchy, easily irritated skin (xerosis of ageing)

**Q10. Why should widespread asteatotic eczema in elderly be investigated?**
- Can be a sign of hypothyroidism, malnutrition (zinc, essential fatty acid deficiency), renal failure, liver disease, drugs (diuretics, statins), lymphoma/ internal malignancy (acquired ichthyosis), HIV — check thyroid, renal/liver function, CBC

## Quick spotter facts
- Crazy-paving fissured shins in elderly in winter — eczema craquelé

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Eczemas). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
